import { Aside, Steps } from "@astrojs/starlight/components";

A theme is the presentation layer of a Plumix site. It holds the templates that turn a resolved request into HTML, along with the design values, head tags and stylesheets those templates read. You declare it once with `defineTheme` and pass it to `plumix.config.ts`.

## What a theme is

A theme is static. `defineTheme` takes a descriptor, validates it and hands the same object back. There is no setup hook and no registration context, so a theme cannot run code at boot the way a plugin does. Everything it contributes is spelled out in the object literal.

A site has one theme, and it arrives through the `theme` slot in `plumix.config.ts`. No plugin can register one.

`templates` is the only required slot. It holds an array of rules built by the [template builders](/themes/templates/), or a bare component as shorthand for a theme with nothing but a catch-all. The rest are optional:

- `document` is the `<head>` descriptor: `title`, `titleTemplate`, `meta`, `link`, `script`, plus attributes for `<html>` and `<body>`, and `canonical: false` for a page that should carry [no canonical link](#opting-a-page-out-of-the-canonical). A template can merge its own fragment over it per render.
- `tokens` are named design values grouped by CSS property, and they are a registry rather than a stylesheet. Plumix emits no CSS for them. Picking a token in the editor writes `var(--plumix-<group>-<slug>, <value>)` into the block's style, where `<group>` is the group name in kebab-case and `<value>` is the token's registered literal, used as the inline fallback. A token registered without a `value` gets the bare reference and no fallback. Your own stylesheet declares the custom property. The known groups are `color`, `spacing`, `fontFamily`, `fontSize`, `fontWeight`, `lineHeight`, `letterSpacing`, `borderWidth`, `borderRadius`, `boxShadow`, `textShadow`, `backgroundImage` and `maxWidth`, and a theme may add a group for any other CSS property.
- `breakpoints` sets the `tablet` and `mobile` max-widths in pixels, defaulting to 991 and 640. The server style emitter and the editor canvas read the same two numbers, so what an author previews is what ships.
- `blocks` and `shortcodes` are presentation components the theme owns. They merge into the per-app registries at boot at the highest precedence, so a theme shortcode replaces a plugin or core shortcode of the same name. A theme block only ever settles against a plugin block, because the `core/` namespace is reserved and `defineTheme` throws on a theme block that claims it.
- `allowedBlocks` lists the blocks the editor allows, site-wide, for a site that offers only its own components and the core blocks it picked. Leave it out and every registered block is allowed. It is an allowlist: a plugin's block is allowed only once the list names it, and a name no one registers is ignored. The theme's own `blocks` are always allowed without being named; set `inserter: false` on one to keep it out of the inserter. A block that only lives inside a parent's slot follows its parent, so `core/columns` brings `core/column` and `core/table` brings its rows and cells. The server holds every writer to the same list, agents included: a save can't add a new instance of a block outside it, while an entry that already holds one keeps it, renders it and saves it. The editor shows such a block with a notice, editable but not duplicated, copied or pasted. Patterns and variations holding a block outside the list are hidden. A block's own `entryTypes` and `capability` narrow the inserter further.

  ```ts
  defineTheme({
    templates: [fallback(Page)],
    allowedBlocks: [
      "core/rich-text",
      "core/button",
      "core/columns",
      "forms/form",
    ],
  });
  ```

- `allowCustomStyles` sets the style policy: whether editors and agents may store custom style values, or only your `tokens`. Leave it out, or set `true`, and every style control takes a custom value. Set `false` and every control offers only tokens: the Custom input is gone, a property whose category has no tokens is hidden, and the Custom CSS and class-name fields are hidden. Keyword options such as border style, alignment and display stay. An array names the categories that keep custom values, and every other category is tokens only. A category is a token group (`color`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, …) or, for a property with no shared group, the property itself (`width`, `height`, `opacity`, …). A value counts as a token only when it names a token the theme declares. The server holds every writer to the same rule: a save can't store a new custom value, a changed one, a token you don't declare, a Custom CSS declaration or a class name. An entry that already stores one keeps it and renders it, and the editor shows it read-only with a way to clear it or pick a token. A value equal to a block's own `defaultStyles` is always allowed, a duplicated or pasted block drops the values the policy refuses, and patterns and variations holding one are hidden from the inserter.

  ```ts
  defineTheme({ allowCustomStyles: false }); // tokens only
  defineTheme({ allowCustomStyles: ["width", "height"] }); // tokens only, except these
  ```

- `redirects` are public-route rules the theme owns, for URL moves that belong to the design rather than to the content model. They lose a tie against `config.redirects` and against plugin-registered rules.
- `css` lists stylesheet paths. The strings never enter the config module graph. The Vite plugin generates a client entry that imports each one, so Vite emits hashed bundles.
- `viewTransitions` turns on the browser's animated transitions between pages. Core emits the CSS rule that enables them, and your stylesheet writes every animation. [Page Transitions](/themes/view-transitions/) covers the setting and has recipes to copy.
- Template dep kinds sit at the top level too, one array of slugs per kind. A theme declaring `settings: ["site"]` has that data loaded and passed into every template's render.

Slugs are yours to choose. One convention is worth knowing: `@plumix/plugin-og` paints its bundled social card from `color.background`, `color.foreground` and `color.muted-foreground`, so a theme spelling those three that way gets a social card in its own palette the moment the plugin is installed. It is all three or none — name two and the card keeps its own — and [the default card's palette](/plugins/og/#the-default-cards-palette) covers the option that points it at whatever your theme calls them instead.

## Quickstart

<Steps>

1. **Write the theme.** Create `theme/index.tsx`:

   ```tsx
   import type { EntryData } from "plumix/theme";
   import { BlockRenderer } from "plumix/blocks/renderer";
   import { defineTemplate, defineTheme, entry, fallback } from "plumix/theme";

   const listing = defineTemplate({
     render: () => (
       <main>
         <h1>Recipes</h1>
       </main>
     ),
   });

   const recipe = defineTemplate<EntryData>({
     render: ({ data }) => (
       <article>
         <h1>{data.entry.title}</h1>
         <BlockRenderer content={data.entry.contentBlocks} />
       </article>
     ),
   });

   export const recipesTheme = defineTheme({
     templates: [fallback(listing), entry(recipe)],
     document: {
       titleTemplate: (title) => (title ? `${title} | Recipes` : "Recipes"),
     },
   });
   ```

2. **Register it.** In `plumix.config.ts`, import `recipesTheme` from `./theme` and pass it as the `theme` slot.

3. **Start the dev server.**

   ```sh
   pnpm dev
   ```

   Sicilian Caponata now renders through the `entry` template at `/recipes/sicilian-caponata`. Every other public URL, the archive at `/recipes` included, falls through to `fallback`.

   The `/recipes/*` routes exist because a plugin registered the `recipe` entry type. A theme targets types, it does not declare them, and [Entry Types](/content-modelling/entry-types/) is where `recipe` comes from.

</Steps>

## What a template receives

`defineTemplate` wraps a render function and brands the result, so the framework can tell a real template from an object that happens to have a `render` key. The render function takes one argument, and most templates destructure it.

`data` is the discriminated union of everything a request can resolve to, keyed by `kind`. Which member arrives depends on which rule matched, and the builder you bind with types it. `ctx` is the request context, carrying `db`, `request`, `user`, `locale`, `config`, `hooks` and the rest. What you wrote in `plumix.config.ts` is read from `ctx.config`, so the base path is `ctx.config.basePath`. Declared template deps arrive as further keys on the same argument, one per kind, each a record keyed by what the template declared — a slug for most kinds, a location id for `menus`.

A template may also carry `document`, either a literal manifest or a function called per request with the same argument `render` sees. Both forms resolve after the walk has picked a winner, and merge over the theme's manifest for that request alone. That is how one page contributes an `og:image` without every page paying for it. The function may be async, and it runs after the template deps and the block loaders on the page's own content, so it can await the same `ctx.memo` lookup a loader made, as [Blocks](/blocks/overview/#a-loader-that-ends-the-request) shows. It may also throw `pageNotFound()` or `redirectTo()` from `plumix/support` to answer the request with the theme's 404 or a redirect instead.

<Aside type="tip" title="A plain component still works">
  A slot accepts a bare React component taking `{data}`. The framework wraps it
  at boot, so it renders inside React's pass and hooks behave. It gets no `ctx`,
  no deps and no `document`, so `defineTemplate` earns its two extra lines on
  any template that needs one of the three.
</Aside>

### Opting a page out of the canonical

Every public page gets `<link rel="canonical" href="…">`, written from the site origin and the request path after every `render:document` subscriber has run. A page that is the canonical address of nothing shareable — an account view, a per-user shortlist — sets `canonical: false` in its `document` and gets none:

```tsx
import type { EntryData } from "plumix/theme";
import { defineTemplate } from "plumix/theme";

export const shortlist = defineTemplate<EntryData>({
  document: ({ data }) =>
    data.entry.slug === "shortlist" ? { canonical: false } : {},
  render: ({ data }) => <main>{data.entry.title}</main>,
});
```

A function decides it per entry, so other entries the same template renders keep their canonical. Set on the theme's `document`, it covers every page, and a template that leaves it unset inherits it. The only value is `false`: a template cannot turn the tag back on with `true`. It stops the automatic tag only. A `<link rel="canonical">` the page declares in `link` still renders, and so does an [SEO plugin](/plugins/seo/) canonical override. A `noindex` page still gets the automatic canonical unless it opts out too.

## The welcome theme

The `theme` slot is optional. A config that omits it gets `welcomeTheme`, a built-in substituted at config resolution, so nothing downstream can tell a theme-less site from one with a theme of its own.

It is the smallest theme there is: one `fallback` rule, one `defineTemplate`, no tokens and no stylesheet. The rendered screen inlines its CSS rather than linking one, so it fetches nothing, and it reads `ctx.locale.code` to pick its strings. Catalogs ship for English, German, Ukrainian, Arabic and Simplified Chinese, but only the English one carries strings today. The other four are empty `.po` files, and `lingui compile` backfills an empty entry with its English source, so every locale renders English until a translator fills one in. It carries a link to `/_plumix/admin`, built through `ctx.config.basePath` so it stays right on a site served from a subdirectory.

Its document manifest sets `robots` to `noindex`. A welcome screen reaching production is a misconfiguration, and search engines should not index one.

<Aside type="caution" title="It answers every public URL">
  A single `fallback` rule matches every resolved node, so a theme-less site
  serves the welcome screen at `/`, at `/recipes` and at
  `/recipes/sicilian-caponata` alike. Published entries are live, and this is
  the screen serving them.
</Aside>

## Rendering entry content

An entry's body is a block tree rather than a string of HTML. Render it with `<BlockRenderer content={...} />` from `plumix/blocks/renderer`. The tree comes off `data.entry.contentBlocks`, which is the stored content narrowed to the block-tree shape, and `null` when there is no content yet or the stored JSON does not match that shape. Pass it to `BlockRenderer` as it is: a `null` renders nothing on the page, and in the editor it still gives the canvas the root it mounts into, so a template that skips `BlockRenderer` for an empty entry leaves a new entry with nowhere to add blocks. The raw `data.entry.content` stays loose so a non-block serializer keeps working. Every node in that tree resolves to one of the specs in [Core Blocks](/blocks/core-blocks/), unless a plugin or the theme registered its own.

The same subpath carries `<Link>` and `<Image>`. `<Link>` takes a resolved entry or term and uses the url already on it, and applies the site's base path to a plain `href`. `<Image>` runs the site's image handling. Reach for both instead of a bare `<a>` or `<img>`.

## Related

Every rule in the `templates` array comes from a builder, and [Templates](/themes/templates/) enumerates all sixteen of them with an example each. [Template Hierarchy](/themes/hierarchy/) is how one of those rules gets picked for a given request, and [Template Data](/themes/template-data/) is the union your render function destructures.

[Custom Rule Kinds](/themes/rule-kinds/) is for the other direction: a plugin adding a slot of its own beside `templates`, resolved by the same walk. The entry types and taxonomies your templates target are declared in a plugin, not in the theme, and [Content Modelling](/content-modelling/overview/) covers how. [Blocks](/blocks/overview/) covers the blocks a theme's pages are built from. The `theme` slot sits beside every other slot in [Configuration](/getting-started/configuration/). A theme's `mail` field restyles the mails core and plugins send, which [Mail](/going-further/mail/) covers.

## Next steps

Read [Templates](/themes/templates/) next, then [Template Hierarchy](/themes/hierarchy/), which together cover what you declare and how a request finds it.

Four further pages in this section are not written yet, and what they cover already ships. Document Manifest goes through `DocumentManifest` and the `theme:document` boot-time filter that lets a plugin contribute head tags. Tokens and Breakpoints covers the token groups above and the `var(--plumix-*)` references a theme declares them for. Component Primitives documents `Link`, `Image`, `PlumixProvider`, the hooks that read its value such as `useUser`, `useTokens` and `useBasePath`, and `useAuth`, which fetches the signed-in visitor on the client. Template Dependencies covers declaring a dep kind on a theme or a template, and the override and extend forms.

When the theme renders, [Routing](/routing/overview/) explains which URLs reach it and [Deployment](/deployment/overview/) takes the result to Cloudflare Workers.
